sections.b: Mark opens with no birth story: "The beginning of the good news" (Mark 1:1), a quotation joining Exodus, Malachi and Isaiah (Mark 1:2–3), John at the Jordan, the baptism with its torn heavens and voice, and two verses on the testing. Then come a day in Capernaum (Mark 1:21–34), five debates that end in a plot to kill Jesus (Mark 2:1–3:6), the choosing of the Twelve and Mark's first "sandwich," with Jesus' family and the scribes from Jerusalem misjudging him (Mark 3:20–35). The opening chapters already show Mark's habits: "right away" eleven times in chapter 1, commands to silence (Mark 1:25, 34, 44; 3:12), and Jesus' strong emotions, which Matthew and Luke often leave out (Mark 1:41, 43; 3:5).

common: Mark was written first, and Matthew and Luke used it.
uncommon: Mark was the last of the three Synoptic Gospels and combined Matthew and Luke (the Griesbach or Two-Gospel view).

sections.b: Mark introduces John through a joined quotation of Exodus 23:20, Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3, all credited to Isaiah (Mark 1:2–3), and describes him in Elijah's clothing (Mark 1:6; 2 Kings 1:8). His message in Mark is brief: a baptism of repentance for forgiveness, and the coming of a stronger one who will baptize in the Holy Spirit, with no "and fire" and no warning to Pharisees as in Matthew and Luke (Mark 1:7–8). His arrest, told only in passing (Mark 1:14), marks the start of Jesus' preaching, and the verb "handed over" links his fate to Jesus' and the disciples' (Mark 9:31; 13:9).

Mark tells the baptism in three verses and without explanation (Mark 1:9–11): John baptizes Jesus "into" the Jordan; as he steps up out of the water he sees the heavens torn open and the Spirit come down into him, and hears the voice, "You are my dearly loved Son." Only Jesus is said to see and hear. Matthew adds John's protest (Matthew 3:14–15), a sign that the church found the baptism of the sinless Jesus hard to explain, which historians take as evidence that it happened. Mark's account was later read by some as Jesus' adoption as Son, a view the church rejected (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.11.7).

Mark announces Jesus as God's Son in his first line (Mark 1:1, though some early manuscripts lack the words), and God says it at the baptism (Mark 1:11). Unclean spirits shout it (Mark 3:11) and are silenced. The title frames the Gospel: God says it again at the transfiguration (Mark 9:7), the high priest asks it (Mark 14:61), and a centurion says it at the cross (Mark 15:39), the first human to do so.

sections.h: The baptism of Jesus as Theophany
sections.b: At the Jordan the Father's voice speaks from the torn heavens, the Son stands in the water, and the Spirit comes down like a dove (Mark 1:10–11). The Orthodox feast of Theophany (January 6) celebrates this as the first clear revealing of the Trinity, and Catholic and Protestant teachers have pointed to it in the same way. Oneness Pentecostals read the scene as one God manifesting himself, and Jehovah's Witnesses as Jehovah, his Son and his active force; see the card on Mark 1.

sections.h: The testing in Mark: two verses
sections.b: Mark gives the testing only two verses (Mark 1:12–13). The Spirit "throws" Jesus into the wilderness (the verb used for throwing out demons), and he is there forty days, tested by Satan, "out among the wild animals," while angels serve him. Mark describes no particular tests and no victory; the struggle continues in the exorcisms (Mark 3:27) and even in Peter's words (Mark 8:33). The wild animals, found only in Mark, have been read as danger, as the peace of a new Adam (Isaiah 11:6–9), or as a word to Christians thrown to beasts under Nero.

Jesus' first words in Mark are a summary of his whole message: "The time has been fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has drawn near. Repent, and believe in the good news" (Mark 1:15). Mark alone has the first line. The verb "has drawn near" has been read as "has arrived" (C. H. Dodd) or "is about to come" (Albert Schweitzer); most interpreters see God's rule already breaking in through Jesus' work, as when he binds the strong man (Mark 3:27), and still to come in fullness (Mark 9:1; 14:25).

Mark has Jesus go up a mountain, summon whom he wants and "make" twelve, "to be with him" and to be sent out to preach and to have authority over demons (Mark 3:13–15). Some important manuscripts add "whom he also named apostles," the wording of Luke 6:13; Mark otherwise uses the word only at Mark 6:30. The list (Mark 3:16–19) puts Peter, James and John first, gives them new names, and ends with Judas "who also handed him over." The number twelve recalls Israel's twelve tribes.

Simon is the first disciple called (Mark 1:16) and the first named in the list of the Twelve, where Jesus gives him the name Peter (Mark 3:16), without the explanation of Matthew 16:18. Mark shows his home in Capernaum, shared with his brother Andrew and his mother-in-law (Mark 1:29–31), and Simon leading the search for Jesus at dawn (Mark 1:36–37). Papias' report that Mark wrote down Peter's preaching may explain why the opening day centers on Peter's town and house.

sections.h: The man made clean in Mark 1
sections.b: Mark tells of a man with skin disease who kneels and says that if Jesus wants to, "you are able to make me clean" (Mark 1:40). Jesus touches him, heals him and sends him to the priest with the offerings of Leviticus 14 (Mark 1:44). Mark's version is the most emotional: Jesus is "angry" in the text followed here (the SBLGNT) or "moved with compassion" in most manuscripts, and he sends the man off sternly (Mark 1:41, 43). The man then spreads the news, so that Jesus must stay outside the towns, as the man once had to (Mark 1:45; Leviticus 13:46).

sections.h: Unclean spirits and a cleansing touch
sections.b: Mark calls demons "unclean spirits" (Mark 1:23; 3:11, 30), using the language of purity, and sets them against the Holy Spirit and "the Holy One of God" (Mark 1:8, 24). When Jesus touches a man with skin disease (Mark 1:41), impurity does not pass to him; cleanness passes to the man. Yet Jesus sends him to the priest as the Law requires (Mark 1:44). Jewish scholars such as Paula Fredriksen stress that the Gospels do not show Jesus rejecting the purity system.

sections.h: The Son of Man's authority on earth
sections.b: Jesus first calls himself the Son of Man in Mark 2:10, claiming "authority to forgive sins here on earth," and again in Mark 2:28, "Lord even over the Sabbath." These sayings echo Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man receives authority from God, but here the authority is exercised on earth. Later sayings speak of the Son of Man's suffering (Mark 8:31) and his coming in glory (Mark 14:62). Geza Vermes read the phrase as a modest Aramaic way of saying "I"; Daniel Boyarin reads it as a claim to divine authority drawn from Daniel.

In Mark 2:1–12 Jesus tells a paralyzed man, "Child, your sins are forgiven," and scribes object that only the one God can forgive sins, echoing the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus heals the man as proof that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive. In Mark 3:28–29 he promises that every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven, except blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

Pharisees first appear in Mark as "the scribes who belonged to the Pharisees" objecting to Jesus' meals with tax collectors and sinners (Mark 2:16). They question his disciples' not fasting (Mark 2:18) and their picking grain on the Sabbath (Mark 2:24), and after the Sabbath healing they plot with the Herodians to destroy him (Mark 3:6). The debates are about holiness at meals, fasting and the Sabbath, matters Pharisees cared about deeply. In Mark, Pharisees play almost no part in Jesus' death, which is driven by the chief priests in Jerusalem.

common: The Pharisees in Mark are Jesus' main opponents in Galilee, but not the ones who bring about his death.

sections.b: Mark sets two Sabbath stories side by side (Mark 2:23–3:6). When Pharisees object to the disciples picking grain, Jesus recalls David eating the Presence Bread and says, "The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings, and not human beings for the sake of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27), a saying with a close parallel in the rabbinic Mekhilta, and found only in Mark. Then he heals a withered hand, asking whether it is right on the Sabbath to save a life or to kill (Mark 3:4). Earlier, the people of Capernaum wait for sunset, when the Sabbath ends, to carry their sick to him (Mark 1:32).

sections.b: When people ask why Jesus' disciples do not fast like John's disciples and the Pharisees, he answers that wedding guests do not fast while the groom is with them, but "days are coming when the groom will be taken away from them," and then they will fast (Mark 2:18–20). It is the first hint of his death in Mark. Early Christians fasted on Wednesdays and Fridays (Didache 8:1).

In Mark, Satan tests Jesus in the wilderness (Mark 1:13), and when scribes from Jerusalem say Jesus throws out demons by Beelzebul, he answers that Satan cannot throw out Satan, and that no one can rob a strong man's house without first tying him up (Mark 3:23–27). The stronger one John promised (Mark 1:7) is binding Satan and freeing his captives, as Isaiah 49:24–25 promised.

Mark alone adds why Jesus warned against blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: "because their claim was, 'He has an unclean spirit'" (Mark 3:30). In Mark's setting the sin is calling the Spirit's work of freeing people the work of an unclean spirit, a deliberate refusal to see God at work. The best manuscripts call it "an eternal sin"; later ones say "eternal judgment" (KJV "eternal damnation").

Mark's first mention of Jesus' family is unflattering: "the people close to him" set out to seize him, saying "He is beside himself" (Mark 3:21), and his mother and brothers arrive and stand outside (Mark 3:31). Jesus names those who do God's will as his brother, sister and mother (Mark 3:35). Some Western manuscripts change Mark 3:21 so that the scribes, not his family, say this. The brothers are named in Mark 6:3.

sections.h: Capernaum and the lake in Mark 1–3
sections.b: Mark's story begins in Galilee: Jesus comes from Nazareth (Mark 1:9), calls fishermen on the shore (Mark 1:16–20), makes Capernaum his base (Mark 1:21; 2:1) and teaches by the sea (Mark 2:13; 3:7). Crowds come from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, across the Jordan and around Tyre and Sidon (Mark 3:7–8).

Mark's first chapter has two famous textual problems. In Mark 1:1, "God's Son" is missing from the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and a few other witnesses; most editions print it, the SBLGNT does not. In Mark 1:41, nearly all manuscripts say Jesus was "moved with compassion," but Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies say he was "angry," which the SBLGNT prints as the harder reading. This site follows NA28 at Mark 1:1 and the SBLGNT at Mark 1:41, with both readings shown.

Mark's opening chapters supply standard evidence for Markan priority. Luke keeps the five debates of Mark 2:1–3:6 in Mark's order (Luke 5:17–6:11); Matthew keeps the first three together (Matthew 9:1–17) and the two Sabbath stories together, later (Matthew 12:1–14). They leave out or soften details that could seem awkward: the Spirit "throwing" Jesus into the wilderness (Mark 1:12), Jesus' anger (Mark 1:41; 3:5), his harsh dismissal of the healed man (Mark 1:43), the name of Abiathar (Mark 2:26), the saying that the Sabbath came into being for human beings (Mark 2:27), and the family's attempt to seize Jesus (Mark 3:21). Supporters of the Griesbach view explain the same places as Mark's own additions.

sections.b: Mark calls the tax collector whom Jesus calls from the toll booth "Levi son of Alphaeus" (Mark 2:14), and then lists a Matthew among the Twelve without mention of Levi (Mark 3:18); Matthew 9:9 tells the same call with the name Matthew.
